vignette:
At 38, she has built a life that looks fast, polished, and controlled from the outside. She works as a stock broker, moving through long days of market openings, client calls, and rapid decisions with the kind of precision people trust with their money. She lives with her partner now, and in the office she is known for staying calm under pressure. It is only after several conversations that the shape of her fear becomes clear, and how long she has been arranging her life around it.

She traces the beginning back about two years, to what first seemed like an ordinary misunderstanding. A client she had worked with only briefly began sending messages after business hours. At first they were flattering, too personal for someone she knew professionally, but easy enough to dismiss. She did not respond. The messages became more frequent. He commented on what she had worn that day, mentioned the coffee shop where she had stopped before work, asked why she had left the office later than usual. The first time she read one of those details, she felt her stomach drop. She remembers standing in her kitchen with her phone in her hand, reading the same line over and over, trying to make it mean something less than what it clearly meant.

After that, she began noticing him everywhere. Across the street from her office building. Parked a few cars behind her at the grocery store. Once, sitting in the lobby of her apartment building as if he belonged there. He never rushed toward her, never did anything dramatic. That almost made it worse. He smiled, nodded, acted as though they shared a private familiarity. She started scanning every reflective surface-shop windows, elevator doors, the black screen of her computer-looking for him before she even realized she was doing it.

At work, she found ways to hide the disruption. She asked a junior colleague to walk her to her car under the pretense of discussing trades. She changed her commute, then changed it again. She stopped posting anything online. She began arriving before sunrise so fewer people would be around the parking garage. In the trading room, where speed and confidence usually come easily to her, she noticed herself losing focus whenever her phone lit up. Her shoulders stayed tight through the day. Sudden movement at the edge of her desk would make her jump. She started making small errors she would normally catch-misreading a number, needing clients to repeat themselves, feeling her mind go blank in the middle of routine explanations.

She did report him. There were meetings with building security, police reports, advice about documentation and personal safety. She saved screenshots and dates in a folder she hated opening. She changed her number, then her route home, then eventually her apartment. Each practical step gave her a brief sense of relief that dissolved quickly. Even after the stalking eased and then seemed to stop, her body did not seem to understand that the danger had passed.

Now, in the present, she lives as if contact could resume at any moment. She checks the locks repeatedly before bed, then lies awake listening for sounds in the hallway. If her partner comes home later than expected, she startles at every noise and feels irritated with herself for needing reassurance. She says she is tired "all the time but never able to rest." Sleep comes in fragments. Some nights she jerks awake convinced someone is outside, her heart racing before she can orient herself. Other nights she dreams that she sees him in a crowd and cannot move.

She avoids places she once moved through without thought. She no longer goes to the gym she used to like because the parking lot feels too exposed. She chooses restaurants with visible exits. She will not sit near windows if she can help it. Her partner gently points out how often she asks who is calling, who is at the door, whether anyone noticed them leaving together. She knows these habits strain the relationship. She worries she has become suspicious, difficult, "not herself." At the same time, she feels angry when others suggest she is overreacting, because part of her still lives in the period when vigilance was the only thing that made sense.

What troubles her most is how the fear has entered her sense of self. She used to think of herself as sharp, independent, hard to rattle. Now she second-guesses her own perceptions and feels ashamed of how quickly her body reacts. In sessions, she often notices the room before she settles into conversation, tracking the door, the hallway, the sounds outside. When she describes her work, she speaks with fluency and command; when she describes leaving the office at dusk, her voice grows quieter, and she rubs her palms together as if trying to warm them. She says she wants her life to feel larger than this constant monitoring. But most days she still moves through the world as though danger is just one unnoticed detail away.
